config.theme: Sprint planning for a payments team at a fictional fintech
config.author: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code session)

cast.theme: Sprint planning for a payments team at a fictional fintech

personas.name: Gemma
personas.role: New engineering manager, joined after the reorg
personas.goals: Earn the team's trust and hit the deadline

personas.name: Mateo
personas.role: Staff engineer, on the team for six years
personas.goals: Protect the team from another impossible plan
personas.hidden_agenda: His best friend was moved to another team in the reorg

personas.name: Aisha
personas.goals: Meet the regulatory deadline at any cost
personas.hidden_agenda: The compliance director reports her progress weekly to the board

pack.title: Payments platform - sprint 9 planning (after the reorg)

agenda.title: The reorg
agenda.goal: Acknowledge the team changes and who owns what now

agenda.title: Instant payments deadline
agenda.goal: Plan the regulatory work against March 31

agenda.title: Tech debt
agenda.goal: Decide what legacy work to keep in flight

agenda.title: On-call
agenda.goal: Make on-call survivable with fewer people

facts.statement: Regulatory fine for missing the deadline = up to $250,000 per month
Test coverage on the payments core = 58%

beats.summary: The elephant in the room; Mateo misremembers the old team size
Instant payments; Aisha's fine figure is inflated and corrected
What to keep in flight; Gemma's coverage number goes unchallenged
Fewer people, same pages; Lukas undercounts the pages, then corrects himself

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Hi, everyone. Sprint nine, and my first planning with you. I know the reorg was hard.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: Hard is one word for it. We were twelve engineers last month. Now we're six.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: The scope didn't shrink, though.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: I want to be honest about what six people can do. I'm not going to pretend.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: Who owns the batch jobs now? Nobody told us.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: We do. All forty-seven of them, unfortunately.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: Forty-seven batch jobs, written by people who aren't here anymore.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: Can we not spend the whole meeting on the reorg? We have a deadline.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: The reorg is why the deadline is a problem.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Both are true. Let's do the deadline, but I'm not ignoring the rest.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: Instant payments has to be live by March thirty-first. If we miss it, the fine is a million a month.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: A million? I thought it was much lower than that.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: The compliance memo says up to two hundred and fifty thousand a month. Still very serious.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: Two fifty. Okay. I'd heard a million in the board meeting.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: Last sprint we did twenty-two points. Instant payments is at least a hundred.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Then it's five sprints, and we have five sprints. With nothing else.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: With nothing else is never true. We have three sev-twos open right now.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: What if we cut the reporting dashboard from instant payments? Regulators don't need it at launch.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: That's maybe fifteen points. It helps.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Then the dashboard comes out of the launch scope. It goes in the first update after March.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: I'll tell the compliance director today that the dashboard moves.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: And the API latency. We're at eight forty milliseconds at p99. Instant payments needs better than that.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: Somebody really ought to profile the payments API before we pile more on it.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: I'll profile it this sprint. It's my code anyway, from before.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Tech debt. Our test coverage on the payments core is about seventy percent, so we're not in terrible shape.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: Seventy is fine for most things.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: The batch jobs have no tests at all. That's where it hurts.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: Can the batch jobs wait until after March?

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: Most of them, yes. Three of them break every month-end. Those can't wait.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Then we fix the three month-end jobs and freeze the rest until April.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: My brother just started a job at a bakery. Four a.m. starts. He says it's still better than on-call.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: He's not wrong.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: Four a.m. every day, though?

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: On-call. Let's talk about it properly.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: Last month we had about fifteen pages. Which is a lot for six people.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: Fifteen? It felt like double.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: You're right, let me look. Thirty-one. Fifteen was the night ones only.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Thirty-one pages for six people is not survivable.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: Could the old team still help with the batch job pages during the transition?

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: I'll ask their manager this week. I'd rather ask than assume.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: And we deploy twice a week. Every deploy is a page risk.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: Maybe we freeze deploys the week before March thirty-first.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Let's see how February goes before we freeze anything.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: Who decided the reorg dates in the first place?

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Mateo, I hear you. I'll carry that upward. That's all for today, everyone. Thank you for being honest with me.

turns.speaker: Lukas
turns.text: Thanks, Gemma.
